meta.description: Charles Dickens wrote it for Tiny Tim in A Christmas Carol, published 19 December 1843. The 1843 text prints no comma - that comes from the book's last line.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'God bless us, every one!'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Dickens. Tiny Tim says it in Stave Three of A Christmas Carol (1843) - without a comma. The comma version is the narrator's closing sentence.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1812–1870 · English novelist · wrote the line for Tiny Tim
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and easy to pin down: Dickens gives the line to Tiny Tim at the Cratchits’ Christmas dinner in Stave Three of A Christmas Carol, published by Chapman & Hall on 19 December 1843, and brings it back as the last sentence of the book. The one thing most people get wrong is the punctuation — the 1843 text prints Tim’s blessing as “God bless us every one!” with no comma.

source.heading: Where the line actually appears

source.excerpt: Then Bob proposed: “A Merry Christmas to us all, my dears. God bless us!” Which all the family re-echoed. “God bless us every one!” said Tiny Tim, the last of all.
trail: The line is spoken at the Cratchits’ Christmas dinner. The 1843 text reads “God bless us every one!” said Tiny Tim, the last of all ↗ — with “every one” as two words and no comma.
Dickens brings it back as the book’s last words. The 1843 facsimile ends: “May that be truly said of us, and all of us! And so, as Tiny Tim observed, God Bless Us, Every One!” ↗
The same Stave Three passage appears in Project Gutenberg’s edition of the novella ↗, and Wikiquote lists both forms among its sourced quotations ↗.
Publication is well documented: Chapman & Hall issued the book on 19 December 1843, with a first run of 6,000 copies that sold out by Christmas Eve ↗.
source.excerptNote: Note the punctuation as first printed: no comma after “us.” The comma-and-capitals form everyone quotes, “God Bless Us, Every One!”, is the book’s final sentence in Stave Five, where the narrator repeats Tim’s blessing back to the reader.

source.rightsNote: The line was first published in A Christmas Carol on 19 December 1843 by Chapman & Hall ↗ — far earlier than 1931, so the work and this sentence are in the public domain in the United States. Dickens wrote in English, so no translation right is involved; Project Gutenberg lists the novella as public domain in the USA ↗. author.name: Charles Dickens
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.bio: Charles John Huffam Dickens was born in Portsmouth on 7 February 1812 and died in Kent on 9 June 1870, having become the most celebrated literary figure of the Victorian era. He worked as a journalist and editor before The Pickwick Papers, Oliver Twist and David Copperfield made serialised fiction a mass medium, and he used that platform to campaign on children’s rights and working conditions. He wrote A Christmas Carol in 1843 after touring the Cornish tin mines, visiting the Field Lane Ragged School and speaking at the Manchester Athenaeum that October, later describing how he “wept and laughed, and wept again” while composing it.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: This one is not a fake — Dickens really wrote it, and it is easy to find in the book. The confusion is about which version you are quoting, and who is speaking it.

items.why: The familiar form with a comma is not what Tim says. At the Cratchits’ dinner the 1843 text reads “God bless us every one!” said Tiny Tim, the last of all ↗ — no comma. The comma and the capitals come from the narrator’s closing sentence in Stave Five: “And so, as Tiny Tim observed, God Bless Us, Every One!” ↗ The version most people quote is a blend of the two.

If you see it set as one word, that is not the 1843 reading — the first edition prints every one as two words both at the Cratchit dinner ↗ and in the closing sentence ↗. The difference is not merely cosmetic: as two words the phrase sits in apposition to “us” and means every one of us, whereas the single word reads as an address flung out at a crowd.

Credited to Tiny Tim, the line is quoted correctly — but Tim is a character, so the words are Dickens’s. This is not Dickens speaking in his own voice in a letter or a speech; it is dialogue he wrote, which he then deliberately handed back to the narrator to close the book ↗.

items.scope: The poem of the same name
items.why: Riley wrote a poem titled “God Bless Us Every One” ↗, and seeing the phrase as a poem title can suggest he coined it. He did not: his opening line quotes Tim by name — “‘God bless us every one!’ prayed Tiny Tim” — so the poem is a tribute built on Dickens’s sentence.

misattribution.truthLine: Charles Dickens wrote it for Tiny Tim in A Christmas Carol, published 19 December 1843. Tim says it without a comma at the Christmas dinner in Stave Three ↗; the narrator gives it back, capitalised, as the last words of the book.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Dickens wrote A Christmas Carol in 1843 after touring the Cornish tin mines, visiting the Field Lane Ragged School and speaking at the Manchester Athenaeum on 5 October 1843 ↗, and Tiny Tim is the argument in miniature: a sick child in a household that cannot afford to make him well. The blessing lands because of who says it. The poorest, frailest person at the table is the one who asks for good fortune on everybody — including, though he does not know it, the employer standing invisibly in the corner.

That is why Dickens repeats it. The Cratchit dinner version is a small domestic moment; the closing sentence is the same words in the narrator’s mouth, capitalised, addressed past Scrooge and out to the reader. Chapman & Hall issued the book on 19 December 1843 with illustrations by John Leech, and the first run of 6,000 copies sold out by Christmas Eve.
context.detailsSummary: The bestseller that lost Dickens money
detailsBody: The book sold out immediately, but Dickens saw little of it. In January 1844 Parley’s Illuminated Library published an unauthorised condensed version for twopence. Dickens sued for copyright infringement and won — and then the publishers declared themselves bankrupt, leaving him to pay £700 in costs, which cut deeply into his already modest profits on the title. Wikipedia’s account of the publication and the lawsuit ↗
One other textual curiosity: the surviving handwritten manuscript does not contain the clause “and to Tiny Tim, who did not die” — that was added later, during the printing process.
context.pull: The poorest person at the table is the one who blesses everybody.

sourcesVerified.claim: The 1843 text of A Christmas Carol, Stave Three, prints Bob Cratchit's toast and then "God bless us every one!" said Tiny Tim, the last of all - with no comma after "us".
The 1843 facsimile edition, Stave Three, prints the same passage and sets "every one" as two words, not "everyone".
The final sentence of the 1843 facsimile, Stave Five, reads: "And so, as Tiny Tim observed, God Bless Us, Every One!"
The 1843 Wikisource text of Stave Five ends: "May that be truly said of us, and all of us! And so, as Tiny Tim observed, God Bless Us, Every One!"
Project Gutenberg's edition of A Christmas Carol contains the Stave Three passage with Bob Cratchit's toast and Tiny Tim's "God bless us every one!"

Project Gutenberg lists the work as "A Christmas Carol in Prose; Being a Ghost Story of Christmas" by Charles Dickens (1812-1870), originally published 1843, copyright status public domain in the USA.
Wikiquote's A Christmas Carol page lists both "God bless us every one!" said Tiny Tim (Stave 3) and the Stave 5 closing repetition among its quotations, and gives 1843 as the publication year.

In early 1843 Dickens toured the Cornish tin mines, and the suffering he saw there "was reinforced by a visit to the Field Lane Ragged School"; after a fundraising speech at the Manchester Athenaeum on 5 October 1843 he concluded a Christmas story would reach a wider audience than a pamphlet. (The article records no 1843 visit to Manchester factories.) A Christmas Carol was first published 19 December 1843 by Chapman & Hall in London, illustrated by John Leech, in a first run of 6,000 copies that sold out by Christmas Eve; in January 1844 Dickens won a copyright suit against Parley's Illuminated Library but the publishers went bankrupt and he paid £700 in costs; the handwritten manuscript lacked the clause "and to Tiny Tim, who did not die," added during printing.

Charles Dickens was born 7 February 1812 in Portsmouth and died 9 June 1870 in Kent; he wrote A Christmas Carol in 1843 and described how he "wept and laughed, and wept again" while writing it. (The article ties the book to a Manchester trip and a Ragged School visit but gives no year for the Manchester trip, so the page follows the dated chronology in the A Christmas Carol article instead.)
Tiny Tim is the character who speaks the line as a blessing at Christmas dinner in Dickens's 1843 novella, and Dickens repeats the phrase at the story's end.

James Whitcomb Riley wrote a poem titled "God Bless Us Every One" whose first line is "'God bless us every one!' prayed Tiny Tim" - explicitly quoting Dickens's character rather than coining the phrase.

The Internet Archive item christmascarolin00dick is a facsimile reproduction of the 1st edition of A Christmas Carol (London, 1843), published c.1920 by The Atlantic Monthly Press with an introduction by A. Edward Newton.

Quote Investigator has no article investigating "God bless us every one" or its attribution to Dickens/Tiny Tim - a site search returns no relevant results, so there is no QI anchor to defer to on this quote.
